issues.legal_issue: An auction purchaser’s application for possession of immovable property bought in execution of a decree is governed by the limitation applicable to delivery of property purchased at an execution sale, rather than the limitation applicable to execution of the decree.
material_facts: The mortgagee decree-holder bought the disputed immovable property at an execution sale.
After the sale was confirmed, the auction purchaser applied for delivery of possession under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The application was filed more than one year after confirmation of the sale.
The lower courts treated the application as one for execution of the decree because of Explanation II to Section 47 of the Code.
issues.conclusion: Article 134 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to an auction purchaser’s application under Order XXI Rule 95 for delivery of possession, with the one-year period running from when the sale becomes absolute. Article 136 does not apply to that application, and Article 134 is not impliedly repealed. On the facts, the application was beyond the applicable period.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 134 and 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963 address different matters: Article 134 governs an application by a purchaser of immovable property at an execution sale for delivery of possession, while Article 136 governs execution of the decree itself. Section 47 and Explanation II to the Code of Civil Procedure determine the forum for questions relating to delivery of possession, but do not convert an application under Order XXI Rule 95 into an application to execute a decree for possession or change the applicable limitation period. The sale must become absolute under Order XXI Rule 92 before an application for delivery can be made; Article 127 separately governs applications to set aside an execution sale. The different scopes of Articles 134 and 136 mean that they do not conflict and that no implied repeal of Article 134 arises.

predicates.auction_sale_delivery_proceeding: An auction purchaser applied for possession of property sold in execution of a decree.
predicates.purchaser_bought_immovable_property_in_d: The property for which possession was sought was immovable property bought by the applicant at the execution sale.

issues.definition: When an auction purchaser seeks possession of immovable property bought at an execution sale, the application is governed by the limitation applicable to delivery of purchased property, not by the limitation for executing the decree.

issues.legal_issue: A later, unmaintainable application to set aside a confirmed execution sale does not postpone the date from which the limitation period for an auction purchaser’s application for possession runs.
material_facts: A judgment-debtor’s application under Order XXI Rule 90 was dismissed for default, and the executing court confirmed the sale.
The confirmation order bound the other parties to the execution proceedings, including another judgment-debtor.

After confirmation, another judgment-debtor filed an application to set aside the sale on grounds outside those in Order XXI Rules 89, 90 and 91; the court dismissed it as not maintainable after confirmation.
The auction purchaser applied for possession within one year of the dismissal of that later application, but more than one year after confirmation of the sale.
issues.conclusion: The later application, being unmaintainable, did not postpone the start of the limitation period. The period under Article 134 ran from the original confirmation of the sale, not from dismissal of the later application.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXI Rule 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, when an application under Rule 89, 90 or 91 is dismissed, the court confirms the sale and the sale becomes absolute, subject to any appeal affecting that order. A later application to set aside the sale that is not maintainable cannot defer the date on which the sale became absolute or restart the period under Article 134 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Chandra Mani Saha v. Anarjan Bibi, AIR 1934 PC 134, recognizes that relevant proceedings, including an appeal from an order refusing to set aside a sale, may affect when a sale becomes absolute; it does not support an unmaintainable later challenge. Kamakshi Ammal v. Arukkani Ammal, AIR 1957 Madras 440, was distinguished because it concerned a claim under Order XXI Rule 58 and a suit challenging the resulting order, which were material proceedings affecting the sale.

predicates.auction_sale_delivery_proceeding: An auction purchaser applied for possession of property sold in execution of a decree.
predicates.sale_confirmed_after_sale_setting_aside_: The court dismissed a permitted application to set aside the sale and then confirmed the sale.
predicates.later_sale_challenge_was_unmaintainable: A party later sought to set aside the confirmed sale through an application that could not be maintained after confirmation.

issues.definition: If an auction purchaser seeks possession after the sale has been confirmed following dismissal of a permitted challenge, an unmaintainable later challenge does not change the date from which the applicable limitation runs.
